newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa cracks down on budget rollovers.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa cracks down on budget rollovers.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel on Thursday announced tough new rules for the rollover of unspent funds from one financial year to another.
Manuel told parliament that a 1992 provision allowing the carry-over of unspent funds from one year to the next "has now become a catch-all for inadequate expenditure planning."
He said his department had on Thursday issued an instruction to all departments setting new rules for the retention of funds unspent when the fiscal year ends on Monday.
"In essence, these provide stringent guidelines as to the use of unspent funds.... rollovers will not be allowed for recurrent expenditure," he said.
In his March 12 budget, Manuel said 14 billion rand had remained unspent on March 31 last year and he authorised the rollover of nine billion rand from fiscal 1995/96 into 1996/97.

Director General of State Expenditure Hannes Smit told Reuters the new rules would significantly cut rollovers, but he declined to estimate how much would be authorised for carry over into fiscal 1997/98.
He said about nine billion rand would remain unspent in the financial year about to end and predicted that the new rules would dramatically slash allowed rollover into 1997/98.
"The new regime is very much stricter than the old system," he said.
"The essence is that all rollovers will be evaluated on the basis of a report that every department has to make on the last day in May about funds unspent on the 31st of March," he said.
Rollovers would be approved only for orders placed prior to March 31 and in the normal course of business, but for which invoices were still outstanding.
"Obviously, if an order is placed on the 31st of March we will not allow that because that would indicate they are just trying to spend at the end of the year," he said.
Smit said the department of state expenditure would make recommendations to the minister of finance, to the treasury committee and to cabinet.
A second provision would allow for rollovers to fund essential services already committed, such as housing subsidies already approved, but not yet paid out.
"There might be cases where we will look at the merits of a particular instance and maybe be lenient, but only for this year because this rule is very new.
"They would have to be very, very special cases that would cause us to deviate from these rules," he said.
